input.text: A teaching text says most millipedes have a cluster of small eyes on each side of the head, and in one of them, Paraspirobolus lucifugus, each eye has about 20 tiny lens units. Other millipedes have no eyes at all, including the flat-backed millipedes (Polydesmida), the order Platydesmida, and the genus Apheloria. Nobody has counted the eyes of most millipede species, so whether you have eyes, and how many, is unknown.
input.note: R3 is from an abstract, so I gave only its lens-unit count, rounded to about 20. I did not say which listed species lack eyes, because no record covers them by name.

input.text: If you are a brown centipede, a review reports that you ran toward a black screen at the side of an arena, so you go for dark places over bright ones. If you are a Chinese red-headed centipede, you avoid sunlight less when your antennae are covered with foil, so your antennae play a part in that. Nobody has measured what a dark shape looks like to you or how sharply you see its edges.
input.note: R1 is from a review abstract (PARTIAL); R2 is about sunlight avoidance, not dark shapes, and the quote does not say antennae sense heat directly, so I kept that claim modest.

input.text: If you are a wild boar, a Bornean bearded pig or an African elephant, your pupil is round, and if you are a hippopotamus, your pupil is horizontal, wider than it is tall. Nobody has recorded the pupil shape of a bear or a kangaroo, and nobody has measured how wide an area your eyes cover around your head.
input.note: No field-of-view record exists for any species in this view; the 240 and 271 degree figures (honey possum, ferret) were left out because numbers do not carry between species.

input.text: Nobody has measured how sharply most reef fish see, and a few measured species differ a lot from one another. A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart. If you are a black-faced blenny, the spacing of the cells in your eye gives 7 to 9, and if you are an Ambon damselfish, a test with striped patterns gave about 1; a review also reports about 3 for the lagoon triggerfish, 7 for the Koran angelfish and 14 for the red grouper.
input.note: Left out R4 (quote gives no value) and R2 (freshwater bass, value and quote disagree). Carried grades not stated in the text, since figures stay with the measured species.

input.text: If you are a Port Jackson shark or a lemon shark, a horizontal streak across your retina holds more densely packed cells, so you see most sharply along a horizontal band. If you are a great white, you have a patch of sharpest vision instead, and it looks at the zone above and to the sides of your head. In most other sharks and rays nobody has mapped the retina, so nobody knows which of these you have.
input.note: Left out R5 (small-spotted catshark): its quote names the species but does not state the value. Left out R1 because it is a skate.

input.text: If you are a black-faced blenny, your eyes are highly mobile, so you can look around at your surroundings without moving your body. If you are a red-black triplefin, you very likely can too, since it belongs to the same genus. For the other reef fish here, nobody has measured how the eyes move.
input.note: The record does not say whether the eyes move independently, so the row does not claim it.

input.text: If you are the coral Acropora millepora, you carry blue-light cryptochromes, and the activity of your gene cry2 rises on full-moon nights compared with new-moon nights. Nobody has measured whether the coral Cycloseris cyclolites or the starlet anemone sense light in this way.
input.note: No record states that these animals lack eyes, so I left "You have no eyes" out. The record also gives no function for cry2, so I made no claim about spawning.

input.text: A slug with no eye stalks can still find the dark end of a chamber: a summary of one study reports this in the slug Limax valentianus. An abstract reports that the great pond snail has light-sensing cells in the skin of its foot, its mantle cavity and around its breathing opening. For nearly every other snail and slug, nobody has measured whether you sense light through your skin.
input.note: R2's value mentions withdrawal at a shadow, but its quote only supports skin photoreceptors, so I left the shadow behavior out.

input.text: The tip of your bill is the part to picture. A review reports very high numbers of touch-sensing units in the bill-tip organ of filter-feeding and dabbling ducks, and you may have them too if you feed that way. Nobody has measured how well you feel with your bill, or how sensitive the rest of your body is to touch.
input.note: R1 names only filter-feeding and dabbling ducks, so geese, swans and divers get no claim; no record gives touch measurements for the rest of the body.

input.text: Records place many of you outside the daylight hours. A compilation of activity records classifies the eastern newt, fire salamander, rough-skinned newt, smooth newt and red salamander as not primarily active by day, and a second compilation scores the great crested newt and the red-backed salamander as nocturnal. Nobody has recorded when many other salamanders and newts are active, so for those species the hours you keep are unknown.
input.note: "Not primarily diurnal" does not say nocturnal, so I kept that wording; R27 scores the red-backed salamander nocturnal although the view lists its diel as unknown.

input.text: If you are a chimpanzee, you see about 65 cycles a degree in the center of your gaze, close to the 60 of a human. If you are a rhesus macaque, a human sees slightly better in bright light and you see better in dim light, and if you are a common marmoset, you see about 30 cycles a degree, half of what a human sees. If you are another macaque or marmoset, you very likely see about as the measured species do, and for many other monkeys and apes nobody has measured how sharply they see.
input.note: Left out other measured species (howler, squirrel monkey, pig-tailed macaque) to keep to three sentences; numbers stay within genus.

input.text: If you are a Mediterranean medicinal leech, a review reports that you have several pigmented eyes on your head, and light-sensing cells without pigment spread across your entire body. For the smooth turtle leech, the North American medicinal leech and the European medicinal leech, the number of eyes is unknown. You may have eyes like these, but nobody has recorded it.
input.note: R1 gives "several" head eyes, no count, so no number is stated; eye counts for the other three species have no record.

input.text: Picture a full circle around your body. A review reports that, based on physiological evidence, scorpions can apparently see 360 degrees around themselves. Nobody has measured how wide a field of view your own species has.
input.note: R1 is a review's statement about scorpions as a group, so I kept it as a report and said the field is unmeasured in your species.

input.text: If you are a Paradesmus gracilis, the one millipede measured so far, a 1951 study found that odors get no response from you, while glucose and sucrose attract you when you touch them. Moisture matters far more in your behavior, and your response to it is purely a change in how fast you move, probably a general effect of dehydration. Nobody has measured how any other millipede senses taste or damp.
input.note: Left out R3 (Polydesmida Tömösváry organs): the row covers all millipedes and the record is only for one order, and it is a thought, not a measurement. Left out the sugar threshold number since it has no job.

input.text: If you are a Caribbean reef octopus, you can see a light flicker at up to about 70 flashes a second in very bright light, a little above the human limit of about 60, and a review reports the same for the common octopus. If you are a bigfin reef squid, your limit is about 50, and if you are a European common cuttlefish, it is below 30. Nobody has measured it in most other octopuses, squid and cuttlefish, including the giant Pacific octopus and the California market squid.
input.note: Kept to measured species because the row grade is i; the cuttlefish record gives only "<30" and the octopus figure was taken at very high light intensity.

input.text: If you are a Heteromitobates discolor guarding your eggs, you use your eyes to find your way back to your clutch, and with your eyes painted over you steer by sensing your own movements instead. A large dark object made a Leiobunum harvestman run away. Nobody has measured how sharply you see or what shapes you can tell apart.
input.note: Left out R3 (negative phototaxis, night activity) to stay within three sentences; its quote is truncated.

input.text: Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all. In eight bat species tested with pigments made in a lab, the ultraviolet-sensing pigment peaks at about 360 nanometers, and a review reports a gene in the Samoan flying fox, Pteropus samoensis, that predicts the same peak. You very likely have this pigment too, but nobody has measured how far into the ultraviolet you see.
input.note: R1 does not list the eight species, so I could not say whether any is a flying fox. R2 is a gene-based prediction, not a measurement. No record gives a spectral range.

input.text: If you are an eastern newt, you steer by Earth's magnetic field, and your compass depends on light. In tests under filtered light, the effect of color on your compass came from two light-sensing mechanisms, one for short wavelengths such as blue and one for long wavelengths, and the two work against each other. Nobody has measured a magnetic sense in any other salamander or newt, so if you are another species, nobody knows whether you have one.
input.note: Left out the pineal organ and the 450 and 500 nm figures: the quote does not name the organ, and the numbers had no job in the row.

input.text: If you are a European common cuttlefish, you have only one visual pigment in your eyes, and a 2020 paper states that cuttlefish have been shown to be color blind. A review lists one pigment for the common octopus and three for the firefly squid. For most other octopuses, squid and cuttlefish, nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have.
input.note: Left out the peak wavelengths (480 to 540 nm) because no human comparison record exists. R2's quote only lists one pigment value for the octopus, so "one pigment" there is a count of the list.

input.text: If you are a goldfish or a rainbow trout, reviews report that you have four kinds of color-sensing cell, where a human has three. If you are a Florida largemouth bass, you have two, and a study found no cell for short wavelengths. For most other fish nobody has measured how many kinds you have, so nobody knows how your colors compare with a human's.
input.note: Left out wavelength peaks (R3, R13, R15 to R19, R22) because they are species-specific and carry no job in a row for all fish.

input.text: If you are a black bear, your retina has two kinds of color-sensing cell, and the long-wave kind outnumbers the short-wave kind at least 3 to 1. A review's table lists the same two kinds in the ferret, a relative of stoats, weasels and polecats, and in a dog the two pigments peak at about 430 and 555 nanometers. If you are another bear, a weasel or an otter, you very likely have two kinds as well, although nobody has measured the cells of a sea otter or a northern river otter.
input.note: Left out a measured claim for the Eurasian otter: the R4 quote is cut off before it states the value.

input.text: If you are a wheat stem rust, one minute of red light promotes the germination of your spores, and one minute of far-red light afterward reverses it. In the mold Neurospora, responses to light fade when the light stays on. Nobody has measured how fast most of you respond to light, or whether you fade the same way.
input.note: No record gives a response time for the pin mold or the bending of stalks, so I left those out.

input.text: If you are a red fox or an Arctic fox, the back of each eye has one small spot, called the area centralis, where the cells that send signals to the brain are packed most tightly. A red fox also has a moderate band of dense cells across the retina, and an Arctic fox's spot is packed more tightly than a red fox's. Nobody has measured this spot in the other foxes.
input.note: Left out R3's "prominent visual streak" for the Arctic fox because its quote does not state it; R1 (dog) not used since it is a different genus.

input.text: You have no eyes, yet light still matters to you: if you are a dog vomit slime mold, a review reports that you cannot form fruiting bodies without it. If you are Physarum polycephalum, a light-sensing pigment called a phytochrome is one way your plasmodium senses light, which makes it break into fragments, and if you are Didymium iridis, you need both starvation and light before you make spores. Nobody has measured how the other slime molds sense light.
input.note: Left out the 680 and 750 nm absorption peaks, since they have no job for a reader.

input.text: A stalk of the mold Phycomyces, raised in the dark, bends toward a light shone from one side, and it uses two separate light systems to do it, one for very dim light and one for bright light. Nobody has measured how faint a light you can sense.
input.note: Left out the number of decades the two systems span, because the record's quote does not state it.

input.text: If you are a lion or a clouded leopard, your eyes have a tapetum lucidum, a layer in the eye that looks milky blue, and a lion's was the largest of the three cats examined in one study. Tigers, leopards, jaguars, snow leopards and Sunda clouded leopards very likely have one too, but nobody has looked for it in mountain lions, cheetahs or jaguarundis. Nobody has measured how little light you need to see.
input.note: Left out the house cat figures (threshold up to 7 times lower than a human's, R2; tapetum reflects up to 130 times more light, R3) because numbers do not carry from house cats to big cats.

input.text: Some bats fly through the dark by sending calls out of the mouth and listening for the echoes. In a flight room, these bats narrowed the beam of their calls when they entered a confined space, and widened it again within dozens of milliseconds when they flew toward open space. Nobody has measured whether you find your way with calls like these.
input.note: R1 covers mouth-emitting bats in general and says nothing about flying foxes, so I left out any claim that flying foxes do or do not echolocate.

input.text: In total darkness, a yellow perch finds prey with its lateral line, and a ruffe finds the same prey from farther away than the perch does. If you are a flavescent peacock, you can detect prey with your lateral line within half a body length. Nobody has measured how well most other fish sense moving water.
input.note: R2 gives no distances, so none are stated for the perch or ruffe. The ruffe is named only as the comparison in R2.

input.text: With your head held still and your eyes looking straight ahead, a human sees about 200 degrees from side to side. Nobody has measured how wide that span is for you.
input.note: Only the human record exists; no primate field width is recorded, so no claim is made about relatives.

input.text: If you are a Daubenton's bat, you can detect a round target 10 centimeters across in very dim light, as measured by testing whether bats found it. If you are another Myotis, a close relative of Daubenton's bat, you very likely see in dim light in a similar way. For bats of other groups, nobody has measured how dim a light you can see by.
input.note: Left out R2 (big brown bat): its value is truncated and the quote gives no light level, so it supports no claim. Left out the threshold number because no record gives a human figure to compare.

input.text: If you are a lone star tick, the abstract of a 1977 electron microscope study reports that your eye is a clear cuticle lens over 30 to 40 light-sensing nerve cells. If you belong to another Amblyomma species, you very likely have the same kind of eye. If you belong to any other kind of tick, nobody has recorded what your eye is made of.
input.note: R1 is an abstract, so the row gives only the lens and the 30 to 40 cells; the pore canals in the value field are left out.

input.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and a compilation of bird eyes reports that a mallard reads about 12, estimated from how densely nerve cells are packed in its retina. If you are a mallard, you see about two fifths of the fine detail a human sees, and if you are a Canada goose, about a third, at 10. The same compilation gives about 11 for the lesser scaup, the greater scaup and the northern shoveler.
input.note: Figures are anatomical estimates from a compilation (Caves 2024); other ducks are not measured or carried here.

input.text: A human stops seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second, and only three reef fish have been measured against that. In bright daylight the spotfin squirrelfish sees flicker up to about 70 flashes a second and the split-banded cardinalfish about 40, and the spiny chromis was measured at about 90. Nobody has measured how fast you see flicker unless you are one of those three.
input.note: Sydney cardinalfish is graded g from R2, but the row stays at i for the view and names only the three measured species.

input.text: If you are a sperm whale or a bowhead, the retina of your eye has only rods and no cones, the cells that sense color. If you are a harbor seal, you have no working short-wave color-sensing cell, and a review table lists manatees with two kinds of cone, one short-wave and one long-wave. Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of most other species here, sea lions among them.
input.note: R1 (fox) and R5 (deer) are other species, so I left them out. The R3 quote is cut off, so the sperm whale claim rests on its value field (rod only).

input.text: If you are a great pond snail, a shadow falling across you makes you withdraw. Your skin senses the change in light, with light-sensing cells located mostly on your foot, inside your mantle cavity and in the skin around your breathing pore.
input.note: R1's value text is cut off; I used only the withdrawal at a shadow and the three body sites stated in the quote.

input.text: A small insect flying a few meters from you may already be close to the limit of what your calls can find. If you are a Kuhl's pipistrelle, a calculation from your measured call levels puts the distance at which you can detect an insect at a few meters. A review reports an estimate of about 20 meters for large objects in Eptesicus bottae, an open-air hunter, but nobody has measured how far you can detect things.
input.note: Rounded R3's 2 to 3.5 m to "a few meters"; its quote is cut off, so I left out the lower-threshold ranges. R8 is an Eptesicus bottae estimate, named as such.

input.text: If you are a castor bean tick, you have strings of light-sensing cells placed on your left and right sides, and a report on that tick says they sense shifts in light intensity. Nobody has measured this in any other tick, so if you are another kind, it is not known whether you have these strings or how well they work.
input.note: R1's quote does not state "no eyes", so I left that claim out. Only Ixodes ricinus has a record; the title "Without eyes" is not backed by a quote.

input.text: If you are an American black bear, you have two kinds of color-sensing cell, and the kind for longer wavelengths outnumbers the other at least three to one. If you are a pig, a review lists two kinds for you as well. Nobody has measured the eyes of a kangaroo, but the tammar wallaby, which belongs to the same genus, has two kinds, so you very likely have two.
input.note: Left out the peak wavelengths (R9 pig, R1 wallaby) since the numbers had no comparison job. Left out the raccoon, which has one cone kind (R6), because it is not a bear, kangaroo or pig.

input.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and the few fish that have been measured differ widely. A goldfish reads about 7, a bluegill about 5 and a zebrafish less than 1, while a review reports about 40 for the rock bass. If you are a fish of any other kind, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
input.note: Left out the largemouth bass record R7 because its quote gives 0.10, not the stated 3.0.

input.text: Cone cells that sense short wavelengths of light, called S cones, have been found in the eyes of a cheetah, a leopard and a bobcat. Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have, or which colors they sense best. A dog, which is a carnivore like you, has two pigments that peak at about 430 and 555 nanometers.
input.note: R1 shows S cones but gives no count of cone classes, so I did not state one for any cat.

input.text: A review reports that alpine, great crested and smooth newts catching prey against a gray card showed that they see color. Fire salamander larvae can tell colored light from white light in behavioral tests. If you are any other salamander or newt, nobody has measured whether you see color.
input.note: R4 quote is cut off, so I left out the retina finding about blue-yellow cells.

input.text: Your eyes face forward, so a wedge of space straight ahead is seen by both of them at once. A review reports that this overlap measures 34 degrees in the Snowy Owl and about 55 degrees in the Australian boobook, and in the Great Horned Owl it measures about 40. The full width of what an owl sees has been measured only in the Tawny Owl, which has a blind area of about 160 degrees behind its head, and nobody has measured it for most other owls.
input.note: Left out any human comparison for binocular overlap, since no record gives a human figure.

input.text: If you are a Virginia opossum or an African elephant, the back of your eye has a tapetum, a light-reflecting layer that sends light back through the retina for a second chance to be sensed. A review reports that the pig and the red kangaroo have no tapetum. Nobody has measured how little light you need to see, and for a bear, a gray kangaroo or most other mammals here, nobody has reported whether a tapetum is there.
input.note: No record gives dim-light sensitivity for any bear, kangaroo or pig, so the row says so. The pig and red kangaroo statement comes from a review quote under a Primates record (R14).

input.text: Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see, and a cone pigment tuned to it, peaking near 355 nanometers, has been cloned from the tiger salamander and tested in cells. Nobody has measured whether your eyes use such a pigment or how well you see ultraviolet. If you are a fire salamander, a test of behavior found high sensitivity in the ultraviolet that comes through your 500 nanometer receptor, with no separate ultraviolet receptor.
input.note: Kept to the grade i wording; the tiger salamander figure comes from a cloned pigment in cells, not from an eye, so I did not carry it to other species as a measured value.

input.text: If you are a European common cuttlefish, a polarized target stays visible in the moving ripples of sunlight that hide a target differing only in brightness. If you are a day octopus, you notice a change of about 1 degree in the angle of polarization, ten times finer than a crayfish manages. Nobody has measured whether you see polarized light if you are one of the squid in this view.
input.note: Left out common octopus anatomy (R1) and Sydney octopus threshold (R3) for length; R2 comparison to crayfish is from its quote.

input.text: If you are a meadow mushroom and your cap is tilted by up to 30 degrees, your gills readjust to the vertical, and if you are a splitgill mushroom, your gills develop facing down in response to gravity. A review of experiments on gilled mushrooms reports that their stems grow away from gravity and their gills toward it. Nobody has measured whether you sense which way is down, unless you are one of those two mushrooms.
input.note: Left out R3 (Coprinopsis cinerea stem bending in 30 minutes) since the species is not on the list; no record covers lichens, so the row does not mention them.

input.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see. No one has tested how much fine detail your eyes can pick out, so there is no number to compare with the 30 cycles a degree that a human reads on an eye chart.
input.note: No records were supplied, so the row only says that acuity is unmeasured and cites nothing; I left out eye structure and any centipede-specific claim. The species list includes the centipede grass orchid (Zeuxine strateumatica), a plant, which looks like a name match by mistake.

input.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a bear, a raccoon, a skunk or a hedgehog, and most other mammals in this group are unmeasured too. Where it has been measured, a wild boar and a western grey kangaroo each see about a third of the fine detail a human sees, and a koala sees about a twelfth. Those figures stay with those species.
input.note: Kept to three measured species for brevity; the elephant, rhinoceros, hippopotamus and opossum values were left out.

input.text: A moth a few long strides away is about as far as a Kuhl's pipistrelle can detect an insect by echo, according to a calculation from its measured calls. A review reports an estimate of about 20 meters for large objects in Eptesicus bottae, a bat that hunts in open air. Nobody has measured how far away you can detect things by echo.
input.note: R3's value text (20 dB SPL) and its quote ("the higher threshold") disagree, so I gave only "a few" strides and left out the exact meters. The Eptesicus bottae figure is an estimate from a review and stays with that species.

input.text: The tip of your bill sits at a set angle in the area your eyes cover, and it was measured from the reflection inside the eye. If you are a mallard, that angle is about 105 degrees. If you are a Canada goose, it is about 80 degrees, smaller than in every other species in the same report.
input.note: The records give only the angle, not what it is measured from, so I left out any claim about seeing below the bill; the title may need a record that defines the angle.

input.text: If you are an Androctonus australis, your median eyes are about 1,000 times more sensitive to light at night than by day, and this change keeps its daily rhythm even in constant darkness. A review reports that the median eyes of some desert scorpions may see well enough to use the horizon for orientation on moonless nights. For every other scorpion, nobody has measured how little light your eyes need.
input.note: Left out the review's pigment-migration claim because its quote does not state it. Only Androctonus australis is measured.

input.text: If you are a big brown bat, your search calls go out 5 to 10 times a second, and each one lasts up to 15 or 20 thousandths of a second. If you are a Mexican free-tailed bat, you call about 4 times a second, with each call lasting about 14 thousandths of a second. For most other bats, nobody has measured how you use your calls.
input.note: Left out R1 (its quote shows "80", the value says 8 degrees), R3 (range depends on threshold), and R6, R7 (group-level beam findings with no named species list).

input.text: Your eyes may sense blue and green light best of all. In Edward's bark scorpion, electrical recordings from the median and side eyes peak at blue (470 nanometers) and green (525 nanometers) and drop much lower for yellow and ultraviolet, and you very likely match it if you are another bark scorpion of the genus Centruroides. Nobody has measured which colors the eyes of other scorpions sense best.
input.note: Only one species (Edward's bark scorpion) is measured; the record gives peak wavelengths but no count of color-sensing cell types, so I made no claim about color vision.

input.text: In a field and flight-room study, bats that send out sound from the mouth narrowed their sound beam when they entered a confined space and widened it again within a few dozen milliseconds when they flew toward open space. Nobody has measured whether you use sound in this way.
input.note: No record covers Rousettus echolocation, so R1 (mouth-emitting bats) is stated only for those bats and the row says plainly that it is unmeasured in you.

input.text: If you are a West Indian fuzzy chiton, the lenses in your ocelli let them work as small camera eyes. If you are a West Indian green chiton, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
input.note: Left out the 9–12 figure: R1's quote gives no unit, and the trait is labeled cycles per degree, which would not fit an angular resolution. Please confirm the unit (likely degrees) before a number is added.

input.text: On many nights, the natural light outdoors is brighter than the dimmest light that a coyote can see, as shown in a test with three coyotes. Coyotes are relatives of yours, but nobody has measured how little light you need to see.
input.note: Only a coyote record exists, and absolute sensitivity does not carry between genera, so the row stays at i and names the coyote result without applying it to foxes.

input.text: If you are a Canada goose, each of your eyes sees a field about 155 degrees wide off to its side. If you are a mallard, a Canada goose or a northern shoveler, your two eyes overlap in front of you over about 20 degrees. Nobody has measured how wide one eye's field is in most other ducks, so nobody can yet say how much of the way around you they cover.
input.note: Left out the mallard single-eye field (R29): its quote is a bare table row that does not label the 183.

input.text: If you are an adult female lone star tick, at least 70 percent of your kind can detect a warm plate 10 centimeters wide from a meter away. If you are an American dog tick, a review reports that unfed adults with their Haller's organs intact move toward infrared light. Nobody has measured whether other ticks sense heat in this way.
input.note: Left out the 37 to 40 °C plate temperature and what organ removal did, since R2's quote only states the result with organs present.

input.text: If you are a common barn owl, a review reports that your two eyes can turn toward each other by no more than about 4 degrees, where a human's can turn up to 30 degrees. In the tawny owl, eye movements were absent or not readily produced by the methods used. Nobody has measured how the eyes of most other owls move.
input.note: R2's quote speaks of "some species" without naming the tawny owl; the tawny owl wording rests on the record's taxon. R3 (head-bobbing) left out as it is not about eye movement.

input.text: One pair of your eyes is easy to spot, and two more pairs are hidden. If you are a European harvestman, a review of gene-expression work reports that one hidden pair is a lateral pair, shrunken and moved inside your body, and the other is an extra pair of median eyes that is just as hard to find.
input.note: R1 is an abstract and its value text is cut off, so the row gives no total count and says nothing about what the hidden eyes sense.

input.text: Nobody has measured how wide an area you take in at once, or how much of it both of your eyes see together. A review reports that the domestic cat, which belongs to a different genus, has about 140 degrees of overlap between its two eyes, and that figure has not been checked in you.
input.note: R1 (domestic cat, 90 degrees out to 30 across the midline) implies far less overlap than R2's 140, so I left R1 out. No record covers any big cat.

input.text: If you are a common octopus, a review reports a horizontal stripe across your retina where light-sensing cells are packed about 55,000 to the square millimeter, against about 20,000 at the edge. If you belong to the genus Octopus or the genus Sepia, you very likely have a stripe too, since one was found in the cuttlefish Sepia esculenta, slightly above the middle of its eye, but if you are a chambered nautilus, your retina has no denser area at all. Nobody has measured this in squid, or in any octopus or cuttlefish outside those two genera.
input.note: Sharpness itself is not in any record, so the row speaks only of cell packing.

input.text: Your eyesight is much blurrier than a human's, who reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart. If you are a red fox, the density of nerve cells in your retina gives an estimate of about 6 cycles a degree, and if you are an arctic fox, about 9. Of the other foxes, nobody has measured how sharply they see.
input.note: Both fox figures are anatomical estimates, not eye-chart tests; the row says so. Gray and island fox are unmeasured, and Vulpes relatives are covered only by the general closing line.

input.text: If you are a Madagascan flying fox, a Greater Mascarene flying fox or a Pteropus rodricensis, you have two kinds of cone, mostly for middle-to-long wavelengths and a few for short wavelengths, which gives you the potential for two-color vision. A rousette, an Eidolon and an Epomophorus fruit bat, each measured in one species, have only the long-wavelength kind and are color blind. Nobody has measured which colors the cones in your eyes sense best.
input.note: Left out R5 (a predicted 360 nm peak in one Pteropus, partial, grade i) and R4 (bats other than Pteropus), since neither measures a flying fox's cone peaks.

input.text: Nobody has measured the dimmest light you can see, in any flying fox or fruit bat. The only bat measured so far is Daubenton's bat, a small insect-eating bat that is not a close relative of yours, so its figure stays with it.
input.note: Only record is a Myotis (different family), so I left out its threshold number; it cannot carry to flying foxes.

input.text: If you are a mallard, a review of earlier measurements reports that your violet-sensitive cone senses light best at about 415 nanometers. Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have, and for most ducks and geese nobody has measured even that one cone. In a Nēnē, a Hawaiian goose, a study found a violet-sensitive cone as well, peaking at about 415 nanometers.
input.note: R1 does not label its other four columns and R2's value is cut off, so I left out the other cone peaks and the cone count. I also rounded the Nēnē's 413 nm to 415.

input.text: Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of a woodlouse like you. A compilation reports that the wharf roach, an isopod and a relative of yours, has three kinds, and one of them senses ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see. Nobody knows whether your own eyes have the same three.
input.note: Left out the 340, 470 and 520 nm values because they belong to the wharf roach alone. R1 and R4 are lizard records and were not used.

input.text: Nobody has looked for the sharpest spot in the eye of most fish, so unless you are one of a few species, nobody knows where yours is. A black-faced blenny has a pit called a fovea toward the top and rear of its retina, a white crappie and a golden shiner each have one patch where cells are packed most densely, and a zebra danio larva has a patch of ultraviolet-sensing cells aimed at the upper front, where ultraviolet-bright prey swim. A review reports a vertical streak instead of a patch in the glyrna.
input.note: Left out the cone densities and the frogfish streak (R6, grade g, not a listed relative); black crappie not named since only the white crappie is measured.

input.text: If you are a leopard slug, you can find your way back to your resting spot from more than 90 centimeters away by smell, moving upwind. You do not need to follow your own slime trail or use vision to do it. For almost every other snail and slug, nobody has measured what you can smell or from how far.
input.note: Left out R2 (sea slugs): its quote only says oral tentacles "probably" sense chemicals and does not mention rhinophores.

input.text: If you are a Pacific crown-of-thorns, the tiny units that make up each of your eyes point about 8 degrees apart, and if you are a blue Linckia, about 16 degrees apart, so the crown-of-thorns sees finer detail, as a review reports. A separate study of juvenile Acanthaster measured about 17 degrees. Nobody has measured this in the purple starfish, the chocolate chip sea star or the Northern Pacific seastar.
input.note: No record states that the eyes sit at the arm tips, so the row leaves that to the title.

input.text: If you are a harbor seal, you can wear a blindfold and still follow the trail a miniature submarine left in the water, using only your whiskers. If you are a northern elephant seal, video from wild seals shows you stretch your whiskers forward ahead of your mouth and catch moving prey by the water movement it makes. Nobody has measured this in the other seals and sea lions.
input.note: Left out the R3 figures (40 m, tens of seconds, 10 to 1,000 Hz): the quote does not name the species and does not state the Hz range.

input.text: In the Madagascan rousette, the Madagascan fruit bat and the Gambian epauletted fruit bat, the retina has one kind of cone, the L-cone, and no S-cones at all, which the researchers describe as color blindness. Nobody has measured the cones of the other flying foxes, such as the straw-colored fruit bat, so for them it is not known whether you have one kind too.
input.note: Graded i for the view; R1 measures only three species, so relatives like Egyptian rousette are not stated as carried.

input.text: Your eyes see far less fine detail than a human's, which read about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart. A review reports about half a cycle a degree if you are a green shore crab, a sixtieth of a human's, and about 1.5 if you are a horned ghost crab, a twentieth. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a Dungeness crab, a Sally Lightfoot crab or a northern kelp crab, among many others.
input.note: Left out the blue crab's 1.8 degree figure (R30) because it is an angle, not cycles per degree, and no record converts it.

input.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see, or how wide an area your eyes take in at once. Your two eyes sit together on a small raised bump on top of your body, and no one has tested what they can make out.
input.note: No records were provided, so I cited none and stated no numbers. The sentence about two eyes on a raised bump is general harvestman anatomy with no record behind it, so please confirm or remove it.

input.text: If you are a nightcrawler, light-sensing cells sit in the skin of every segment of your body, and they are most plentiful where your skin is most sensitive to light. In a flatworm called Schmidtea mediterranea, worms with their eyes removed or their heads cut off still shy away from near-ultraviolet light, so the skin and body sense it without eyes. Nobody has measured whether you sense light through your body in this way if you are any other kind of worm or leech.
input.note: Left out any claim that all these worms lack eyes, since no record says so and some flatworms, fanworms and leeches have them.

input.text: If you are a fire salamander, your eye shifts its focus toward near just before you catch prey, and you use that shift to judge how far away the prey is. If you are a great crested newt, your eye can change its focus only very weakly, and in air you are short-sighted. For most other salamanders and newts, nobody has measured how you judge distance.
input.note: Left out the diopter figures for the great crested newt, since they have no job for a reader. Relatives in Triturus and Salamandra are covered only by the "most other" wording.

input.text: If you are a strawberry conch, you see about 1 cycle per degree, which is about a thirtieth of the 30 cycles per degree a human reads on an eye chart. If you are a common periwinkle, a review lists an estimate for Littorina, your genus, made from the anatomy of its eye, and you very likely have the sharpness of that genus.
input.note: I left out R2's value (0.113): the quoted table line does not state it, so the periwinkle half gives no figure.

input.text: Beside the lateral line organs of salamanders and newts, an anatomical study found smaller pit organs, each served by one nerve fiber, and it considers them electroreceptors. The olm, a cave salamander, has been shown to sense a slowly moving direct-current field and its polarity, and a meeting abstract reports that amphiumas showed behavioral responses, likely feeding responses, to electrical signals. Nobody has measured whether you sense electricity.
input.note: Left out the olm's threshold figure (0.5 mV/cm) since it has no comparison job and belongs only to the olm.

input.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see, whether you are a hammerhead flatworm, a stripe-bellied flatworm or Schmidtea lugubris. A review of animal eyes lists one figure for a flatworm it calls Planaria, and that figure cannot be passed on to your genus.
input.note: Left out numbers: R1's quote ("0.8 35 A") does not state 0.014 cycles per degree, and R2's quote gives 73° with no sign it is an acuity.

input.text: The patch of space ahead where both your eyes see at once varies a lot from one species to the next. It is about 10 degrees wide in a lemon shark, 11 in a blacknose shark, 13 in a bonnethead, 35 in a scalloped hammerhead and 50 in a winghead shark, and in rays it is about 45 in a cow-nosed ray and 70 in an Atlantic stingray. Nobody has measured it in most other sharks and rays, so if you are not one of these, nobody knows how much your two eyes overlap.
input.note: No human overlap figure in the records, so no human comparison. Eye placement left out for lack of a record.

input.text: The shore crab Hemigrapsus sanguineus has one kind of color-sensing cell that peaks in violet-blue light, at about 440 nanometers, and one that peaks in green, at about 510. Four fiddler crab species have a single kind of cell, peaking between 510 and 530. Nobody has measured whether you have a cell that senses ultraviolet, the light just beyond violet.
input.note: No record gives a crab cell peaking below 400 nm, so the row states the gap. Mantis shrimp UV records (R4, R13) left out because they are not crabs.

input.text: If you are a land snail or slug, a review reports that your eyes are camera eyes whose optics cannot focus an image on their shallow retinas. If you are a periwinkle, a review reports that your lens forms a sharp image, and if you are a nudibranch, your small eyes sit deep inside your body and tell light from dark without seeing images. For most species, nobody has counted how many eyes you have or measured what kind they are.
input.note: No record gives eye counts for any species, so the count is stated as unmeasured.

input.text: If you are a nightcrawler, you react negatively to light of ordinary brightness and move away from it. If you are a Mediterranean medicinal leech, the response of your S cell system to light depends strongly on how large an area is lit, and your adjustment to brightness happens locally. Nobody has measured how the other worms and leeches react to bright and dim light.
input.note: Left out the nightcrawler's attraction to very dim light (R3 quote does not state it) and the planarian UV result (R2, Schmidtea is not a listed species or genus).

input.text: If you are a bay scallop, your eyes can separate two details only when they are about 2 degrees apart, the width of a human thumb held at arm's length. If you are a small giant clam, you pull in your mantle when a dark spot is about 13 degrees wide, which is more than six thumbs side by side, and a spot a little under 12 degrees does not make you pull in.
input.note: Left out king scallop: R3's quote is a table line that does not state the 0.314 value, so no figure is given for it.

input.text: If you are a platypus, the back of your eye is mostly rod cells, the kind that work in dim light, with a minority of cone cells that test positive for red-sensing and blue-sensing pigment, so you have two kinds of color-sensing cell where a human has three. Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of an echidna, so what you see in color is unknown if you are one. Nobody has measured it in a close relative either.
input.note: Left out the 550 and 451 nm peaks (R2, R3): the quote names no species and both records carry the same quote, and the row grade lists wavelength as unknown.

input.text: Ultraviolet, light that humans cannot see at all, is what the eyes of one harvestman, Megalopsalis tumida, sense best, with a second broad peak from blue to green. A 1988 report found that its eyes responded across at least a hundred-thousandfold range of light intensity. For other harvestmen, including you if you belong to another species, nobody has measured which colors you sense or how dim a light you can use.
input.note: Only Megalopsalis tumida is measured; the R2 value text was truncated, so I used only the quoted 5 log units and left out the phototaxis claim.

input.text: If you are a European medicinal leech, touch-sensing cells in your body wall respond to stimulation repeated up to about 50 to 60 times a second, as an abstract of a 1969 study reports. Nobody has measured how any other worm or leech senses touch, so for you it is unknown.
input.note: Only touch is supported; no records for taste or damp, so those are left out of the row despite the title.

input.text: Your whole order, the Geophilomorpha, lives underground. A commentary on the genome of the maritime centipede calls all of its members blind, which means you very likely have no eyes at all. That commentary lists no eye count for each species, so a count for your own species is not on record here.
input.note: R1 says all Geophilomorpha are blind (audited m), but the row grade is i, so I hedged to "very likely" and noted that no per-species count is recorded. You may want to regrade.

input.text: Your pupil is a horizontal slit if you are an eastern newt, a smooth newt or a red salamander, and it is round if you are a fire salamander or a rough-skinned newt. If you are an eastern newt, the spacing of the signal-sending cells in your retina puts your sharpness at about 2 cycles a degree at best, where a human reads about 30. Nobody has measured how sharply the other salamanders and newts see, and nobody has measured how wide a field any of you sees.
input.note: Left out the crested newt acuity (R2): its quote does not state the value, and it is another genus. Pupil shape differs even within a genus (smooth vs. Carpathian newt), so I named species only.

input.text: Where sharpness has been measured in sharks, it comes out well below the 30 cycles a degree that a human reads on an eye chart. If you are a great white shark, the retinas of two young ones give an upper limit of about 5 cycles a degree, and a review reports 11 for the bigeye thresher and 2 for the brown-banded bamboo shark. For most other sharks and rays, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
input.note: Left out Port Jackson, wobbegong, epaulette, skate and stingray figures to keep the row short; the row stays at i because most species are unmeasured.

input.text: Along each side of your head sit several small eyes. A survey of 353 scorpions from 20 species and 8 genera of the family Buthidae, which includes the bark scorpions, found 5 pairs of lateral eyes, where earlier works had reported 3 pairs. The survey does not say which species it counted, so how many lateral eyes you have is still open.
input.note: R1 is a family-level survey with no species named, so I left the count open for each listed species; "lateral eyes" only, since no record covers the median eyes.

input.text: If you are a European common cuttlefish, a review reports that your pupil is a horizontal slit with a W shape in bright light, and that it turns circular in darkness. Nobody has measured the pupil of the other octopuses, squid and cuttlefish, so if you are one of them, nobody knows what shape yours takes.
input.note: Only Sepia officinalis has a record, and it is partial (a review), so the shape is not carried to other cuttlefish genera.

input.text: A study that sequenced the retinas of six owl species found no sign of the cell that senses violet or ultraviolet light. Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have, so nobody can say which colors you tell apart.
input.note: Left out R1 (tawny owl 463 nm): the number has no comparison job and the quote gives no column labels.

input.text: Sharpness. If you are an African bush elephant, you see a little under half the fine detail a human sees. A calculation from how densely the cells that carry signals out of your eye are packed in your retina gives your best sharpness as about 14 cycles a degree, where a human reads about 30 on an eye chart.
input.note: Value is an anatomical estimate (13.16 to 14.37), so the row says it is calculated; no other elephant species has a record.

input.text: If you are a staghorn coral of the species Acropora millepora, your cells make a blue-light sensing protein called cryptochrome, and the amount of one kind, cry2, rises on full-moon nights compared with new-moon nights. Nobody has measured this in Cycloseris cyclolites, a mushroom coral, so nobody knows whether you sense moonlight the same way.
input.note: R1 does not say the cells sense the moon directly or that cry2 drives spawning; the row states only the expression change. Common names for the two species are not in the records, so "staghorn coral" and "mushroom coral" may need checking.

input.text: If you are a Turkish snail, your eye senses light best in the blue-green, near 496 nanometers, and an abstract reports two kinds of cell with peaks between 465 and 500 nanometers. If you are a Limax slug, four light-sensing proteins have been found in the genus, with peaks between about 455 and 500 nanometers, and the eye of Limax valentianus senses light best near 480. Nobody has measured the eyes of most snails and slugs, and nobody has shown whether you tell one color from another.
input.note: Left out how the Limax opsins are arranged across cells, since the R4 quote does not state it. Also left out the UV sensitivity detail beyond the peaks.

input.text: A review reports that owls have outer ears hidden beneath the feathers of the facial disc, and that some species can hunt by hearing alone. If you are a barn owl, your best hearing threshold is about 20 decibels more sensitive than other birds', and if you are a great gray owl, you can plunge through snow onto prey you cannot see. Nobody has measured how well most other owls hear.
input.note: Hearing is measured only in the barn owl and the great gray owl, so the barn owl figure stays with that species.

input.text: If you are a house centipede, your brain has well-developed centers for smell and for touch. If you are a brown centipede, one study found evidence that pores at the base of your legs release a scent that differs between males and females. Nobody has measured how faint a smell you can detect or how light a touch you can feel.
input.note: Left out R5 (genome commentary on Strigamia, grade g) and the plant records R1, R4; no record measures touch sensitivity in any centipede.

input.text: Picture a worm lying still on wet leaves, and another one crawling beside it. Nobody has measured whether you see the two differently, so nobody knows if a still thing stays hidden from you.
input.note: No records were supplied, so the row states only the unknown and cites nothing; any claim about motion sensing was left out.

input.text: If you are a house centipede, Scutigera coleoptrata, recordings from the retina of your eye found two peaks of sensitivity, one in blue light near 450 nanometers and one in ultraviolet near 350 nanometers. The researchers expect you have at least two kinds of visual pigment. Nobody has measured the color sense of any other centipede.
input.note: Only Scutigera coleoptrata has records; the row says nothing about other Scutigera species or other orders.

input.text: If you are a Paradesmus gracilis, touch dominates your behavior, and you have tactile hairs on your legs, the sides of your body and especially your antennae. A description of the order Polydesmida says a walking millipede taps the ground continuously with the tips of its antennae. Nobody has measured how light a touch you can feel.
input.note: R1 quote is cut off, so I used only the hair locations and the claim that contact reactions dominate behavior. R2's count of antennal tip structures is cut off, so I left it out.

input.text: Picture the darkest night in which you can still see anything. Nobody has measured how faint a light you can see in that dark, in Azara's night monkey, the douroucouli or any other night monkey, so nobody can say how your threshold compares with a human's, which has been measured.
input.note: Only a human record exists; its unit is not in the quote, so I left the number out and claimed nothing about night monkeys being active at night.

input.text: If you are a dog vomit slime mold, a review reports that your plasmodium cannot fruit without light. In another slime mold, Physarum polycephalum, a light-sensing molecule called a phytochrome is one of the receptors that makes the plasmodium break into pieces in light. Nobody has measured how fast you respond to light.
input.note: No record gives a response time for any slime mould, so the row says so. R3 (Didymium iridis) was left out for length.

input.text: Polarized light is light whose waves vibrate in one direction, and fiddler crabs, mantis shrimp and the tawny hermit crab have all been shown to see it. The tawny hermit crab and two other hermit crabs spotted predator-like shapes by polarization contrast alone. If you are not one of the crabs that were tested, nobody has measured whether you see it.
input.note: Left out the common mud crab result (R5, gaze steadied by brightness cues) and the signal crayfish anatomy (R7, suggestion only).

input.text: If you are a harbor seal, you have one kind of color-sensing cell, where a human has three, and the short-wave kind found in many mammals is missing from your retina. If you are a bowhead or a sperm whale, you have no working cones at all and only rods. Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of most other seals, sea lions, whales and dolphins.
input.note: Left out dolphin/porpoise cone peaks (R3, R11) and the partial manatee table (R13); R2, R4, R12 are dog, pig and deer records and were not used for seals or whales.

input.text: Humans have three kinds of color-sensing cell, and the reef fish measured so far have three or four. A review reports four kinds in the threespot damselfish, the black-tailed dascyllus and the blue-green chromis, and in the damselfish Pomacentrus amboinensis one of the four senses ultraviolet, which humans cannot see, while the lagoon triggerfish has three. For most other reef fish, nobody has measured how many kinds you have.
input.note: Left out R3 and R4 (largemouth bass, a freshwater fish); no record supports carrying its pigment peak or cell count to reef fish.

input.text: Nobody has measured how your eyes guide you toward dark places. Nobody has measured how much light it takes to change what you do, in any woodlouse or its close relatives.
input.note: Only record (R1) is a rattlesnake study and says nothing about woodlice, so I wrote an i row with no claims and no citations.

input.text: You have no eyes, yet some fungi sense light anyway. If you are an oyster mushroom, blue light strongly speeds the growth of your stalk, cap and gills, and if you are a king trumpet mushroom, your young buds develop faster under blue light than under red. For most other fungi and lichens, nobody has measured how you sense light.
input.note: Left out the lichen, rust and mold records because their values are cut off or need more space than three sentences allow.

input.text: In a two-chamber test, a slime mold called Physarum polycephalum was attracted by glucose, galactose, phosphates and ATP, and repelled by sucrose, fructose and some mineral salts. Nobody has measured which chemicals attract or repel you.
input.note: Only one species (Physarum polycephalum) has a record; chemical carry across species is not allowed, so the row stays at i.

input.text: If you are a blacklegged tick, the sensing organs in your Haller's organ respond most to m-cresol and next to p-cresol, and if you are a lone star tick, your cells respond to carbon dioxide for longer after you have been in air low in it. If you are a castor bean tick, you spend less time questing as the air dries. Nobody has measured whether you sense vibration, such as footsteps, and for most ticks nobody has measured smell either.
input.note: No record covers vibration in any tick, so the row says it is unmeasured. R1 and R3 are abstracts, so I gave only what they state.

input.text: If you are an American dog tick, an adult released in a field moves toward road edges, and an adult with its eyes removed does this less. Nobody has measured what shapes you can make out, and no other tick has been tested this way.
input.note: R1 shows eyes matter for moving toward road edges but does not say what shapes a tick sees, so I left out any claim about shape or sharpness.

input.text: Nobody has measured how fast a light can flash before your eyes stop seeing the flicker, and that is true for most crabs. Dampier's fiddler crab follows flicker up to about 75 flashes a second by day and about 60 at night, and a review reports about 14 for the deep-sea crab Bathynectes longipes. Humans stop seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second.
input.note: No flicker measurement exists in the records for the commonly met crabs, so the row names the two measured crabs only.

input.text: In two bats, Glossophaga soricina and Carollia perspicillata, researchers found two kinds of color-sensing cell in the eye. In eight bat species, a pigment made in the lab sensed ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see. Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of most bats, so nobody knows how many kinds you have.
input.note: R2 does not name the eight species in the quote, so the row does not say which they are; the 357 to 359 nm figure was left out as it has no job.

input.text: Colors. If you are a tammar wallaby, you have two kinds of color-sensing cone, where humans have three, and a review reports their peak sensitivity at 420 and 539 nanometers, in the violet-blue and the green. Other kangaroos and wallabies of your genus have not been measured, but you very likely have two kinds as well.
input.note: Peak wavelengths are only in a partial review record for the tammar wallaby; I gave them only for that species. Rule 2 lets only the number of classes travel, so the peaks are not carried to the other kangaroos.

input.text: If you are an Asian moon jellyfish, you pulse faster in light, and you spend more time in the lit side of a tank than in the dark side. That was measured in juveniles. Nobody has measured this in the greater moon jellyfish or the moon jellyfish, so for you the question is still open.
input.note: Only R1 (Aurelia coerulea juveniles) supports a claim; no records for A. labiata or A. aurita, so they are stated as unmeasured.

input.text: How sharply you see depends on which animal you are: if you are a common octopus, a review reports about 45 cycles a degree, finer than a human's 30, while for a pale octopus the same review reports only 3 to 7. If you are a bigfin reef squid, you see about 2 cycles a degree at 2 months old, and if you are a European common cuttlefish, you can tell two stripes apart only when they are about half a degree apart. If you are a chambered nautilus, the stripes must be 5 to 11 degrees apart, and nobody has measured this in most other species.
input.note: Left out R6 (Octopus tetricus 0.3 cpd is a contrast-sensitivity peak, not an acuity limit) and R3 (decimal acuity, not given in cycles a degree).

input.text: Your skin may sense light with no eye involved. If you are a greenhouse millipede, a 1951 experiment found that your skin senses light and that light changes how much you move, with no steering toward or away from it. Nobody has measured whether other millipedes sense light through the skin.
input.note: R1's quote mentions "both species" without naming the second, so I named only the greenhouse millipede. It does not say whether light speeds you up or slows you down, so I left that out.

input.text: If you are a European woodlouse (Porcellio scaber), your eyes are made of many small units, and each unit has its own curved lens with a round crystalline cone beneath it. Other Porcellio woodlice very likely have the same kind of eye. For most other woodlice and relatives, nobody has examined the eye, so its kind is unknown.
input.note: R2 also names Armadillidium vulgare, but the view marks its eye type unknown, so I stated it only for Porcellio scaber. R1 is a skink and was not used.

input.text: Imagine flying home across dark country with a compass that needs setting at sunset. If you are a greater mouse-eared bat, you use a magnetic compass, and you calibrate it with cues from the sky at sunset. Nobody has measured whether other bats sense the magnetic field at all.
input.note: Only R1 (Myotis myotis) supports this row; the other species stay unmeasured, so I stated that plainly and gave no numbers.

input.text: Red light falls on you along with every other color, and nobody has measured whether you sense it. In the red bread mold, the light that works best at starting carotenoid pigment production is blue, and a review reports that the pin mold Phycomyces bends toward blue light most strongly as well.
input.note: No record tests red light directly, so the row only says the two measured molds peak in blue and that red is unmeasured. Wavelength numbers left out because they do no comparing.

input.text: Picture a slime mold that has eaten everything around it and is starting to run out of food. In Physarum polycephalum and Didymium iridis, starvation and light are both needed to start spore-making, and a 1950 review reports that the dog vomit slime mold cannot fruit without light. Nobody has measured this in the other slime molds, so if you are not one of these three, nobody knows whether you need light to fruit.
input.note: R1 (phytochrome in Physarum) concerns plasmodium fragmentation, not hunger, so I left it out.

input.text: If you are a cheetah, the color-sensing cells called M cones lie in a horizontal streak across your eye, the pattern also found in the pig and the deer, which live in open country. A compiled value puts your sharpness at about 25 cycles a degree, a little under the 30 a human reads on an eye chart.
input.note: R1's method is not stated, so I gave the sharpness as a compiled value. R2 gives the streak but not that it is the sharpest region, so I did not say that.

input.text: If you are a Canada goose, the tip of your bill projects at about 80 degrees, the smallest angle measured in any of these geese and swans. If you are a pink-footed goose it is about 100 degrees, and if you are a brant it is about 115. Nobody has measured it in the mute swan, the greylag goose or several other geese and swans.
input.note: Records give only the angle value, not its reference direction, so the row does not say what 80 degrees is measured from.

input.text: In the harvestman Iporangaia pustulosa, an abstract reports that live isopods were noticed only on contact, mainly by the first pair of legs. In the harvestman Discocyrtus pectinifemur, tests showed that it smells fresh dead prey through a mesh and stays near it. Nobody has measured how you sense touch or smell, so neither result can be said to be yours.
input.note: Both records come from other harvestman species, so the row stays grade i. Taste by contact is not covered by any record, so I wrote smell only.

input.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see. The only close relative in the records is a different kind of isopod, Natatolana borealis, and a compilation of eye measurements gives its compound eye about 0.05 cycles per degree, where a human reads about 30.
input.note: Left out R3 (Cirolana): its quote does not state the 0.033 value. R2 is a lizard.

input.text: How sharply you see depends on which owl you are. A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and a review reports only 4 for a common barn owl, while a tawny owl tested on behavior reads about 11. Estimates from counts of retinal cells give about 15 for a burrowing owl, 25 for a great gray owl, 30 for a great horned owl and 40 for a snowy owl, which is as sharp as a human or a little sharper.
input.note: Barn owl figures differ: 4 cpd (R1, common barn owl, review) and 13.6 (R5, American barn owl, retinal estimate); I used only R1. Owls with no record (screech owls, saw-whet, etc.) are not covered.

input.text: If you are the coral Acropora millepora, you have no eyes, yet your cells make a blue-light sensing protein called cryptochrome. The gene for one kind, cry2, switches on more on full-moon nights than on new-moon nights, so your body can tell a bright night from a dark one. Nobody has measured this in Cycloseris cyclolites, a mushroom coral.
input.note: R1 measures gene expression only; the quote does not say the coral's spawning depends on it, so the row stops short of that. Cycloseris is described as unmeasured, with no claim about its biology.

input.text: When your pupils narrow in bright light, they close to a tall, thin slit. A published classification records vertical pupils in the clouded leopard, and the Sunda clouded leopard belongs to the same genus, Neofelis, so if you are a Sunda clouded leopard you very likely have them too.
input.note: R1's quote is only a table row label ("Neofelis_nebulosa 322"), so the value "Vertical" rests on the record's value field. I left out slit width, pupil size and any claim about why the shape helps, since no record gives them.

input.text: If you are a cheetah, a review lists your eyesight at 23 cycles a degree, a little below the 30 a human reads on an eye chart. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar or any other big cat. A 1942 textbook says only that the great cats have high visual acuity, and it gives no measurement.
input.note: Cheetah value is a compiled figure with no method stated; the house cat figure (R1) was left out because acuity numbers do not travel across genera.

input.text: Measured fish differ widely in the fastest flicker they can see. Reviews report about 25 flashes a second for the painted comber, about 65 for the goldfish and more than 100 for the flathead mullet, against about 60 for a human. Nobody has measured how fast you see flicker if you are a bluegill, a bass, a carp or one of many other fish, and the measured species differ too much to guess.
input.note: Left out the Atlantic salmon figure (R11) because numbers do not carry to brown trout, and the eel figure because it is behavioral.

input.text: Monkeys and apes differ in how many kinds of color-sensing cell they have, and for most of you nobody has measured it. If you are a crab-eating macaque, your three kinds peak near 430, 530 and 560 nanometers, and a review reports three kinds in macaques generally, so other macaques very likely have three as well. Howler monkeys have three in both males and females, so a howler very likely has three, while a review reports that squirrel monkeys have two, or three in some females, and ring-tailed lemurs have two.
input.note: Left out the human peak numbers (R1) for the monkeys, since no record says they carry over; baboons, vervets, capuchins, spider monkeys and marmosets are covered only by the opening sentence.

input.text: A light flashing once every two seconds is already too fast for the crown-of-thorns starfish, a different sea star, to see as separate flashes, where a human stops seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second. A paper reports that this is the slowest flicker limit measured in any animal eye, and it belongs to that starfish alone. Nobody has measured how fast a flicker you can see.
input.note: Flicker figure is from a different genus (Acanthaster), so it is shown only as that species' value; the row has no record for color, so "gray" is not claimed.

input.text: A network of the wood-rot fungus Phanerochaete velutina, moved to new soil, regrew mostly from the side that had faced the bait. The authors read this as a memory of which way it had been growing. Nobody has measured whether you sense chemicals from food, or how you find it.
input.note: R1's quote shows memory of growth direction, not chemical sensing, so I left out any claim about how you sense food chemicals.

input.text: A human thumb held at arm's length covers about 2 degrees, and you need a target many thumbs wide before you can pick it out. If you are a Atlantic purple sea urchin, you turned toward targets only when they were 45 degrees wide or more, and if you are a Diadema africanum, a modeling paper reports you move toward dark objects only when they are 30 to 70 degrees wide, which is 0.01 to 0.03 cycles a degree where a human reads about 30. If you are a Pacific purple sea urchin, the spacing of your spines predicts a sharpest detail of about 8 to 11 degrees, and if you are an Arctic green sea urchin, you very likely see about as coarsely as that close relative.
input.note: Fixed "a Atlantic" grammar not possible after submit; R3 is an anatomical prediction, so worded as a prediction. R2 is secondhand via a modeling paper.

input.text: If you are a platypus, you hunt underwater with your eyes and ears closed, and a review reports that electroreceptor organs and touch-sensing organs in the skin of your bill are what you use to locate prey. If you are a short-beaked echidna, nobody has measured whether you have an electric sense.
input.note: Only the platypus has a record; no record covers bears, kangaroos, pigs or other mammals, so the row says nothing about them.

input.text: If you are a house centipede, each of your eyes is a small triangle of about 150 tiny units, and each unit has its own cornea and a crystal cone under it; if you are a Scutigera forceps, each eye has about 200. If you belong to the order Geophilomorpha, the centipedes that live underground, you are blind. For most other centipedes, nobody has counted the eyes or described what kind they are.
input.note: Left out R6 (four ocelli per side) because its quote says "other species" without naming the group, and R5/R7 (blind scolopendromorphs) because they do not state a count for a named species.

input.text: If you are a smooth newt, you use ultraviolet light to hunt while you are a larva. Larvae raised without ultraviolet made less of the protein that senses it and caught prey less, so how well you sense ultraviolet depends on the light you grow up in. Nobody has measured this in palmate, Bosca's or Carpathian newts.
input.note: R1's value is cut off after "caught prey less", so I gave no catch rate or size of the effect.

input.text: In the dark, a Lake Malawi cichlid called Aulonocara stuartgranti can find live prey within about half a body length using its lateral line system. That fish lives in a lake, and nobody has measured how well you sense moving water.
input.note: Only record is a freshwater cichlid, so the row names it and does not carry its figure to reef fish.

input.text: Nobody has examined the eyes of the red swamp crawfish, the signal crayfish or the yabby closely enough to say what kind of eye you have. A review reports that many adult crabs keep apposition eyes, and a study of three slipper lobsters found a superposition eye with square facets. Nobody has measured whether a crayfish eye matches either one.
input.note: R1's value text mentions shrimps with reflecting eyes, but its quote does not state it, so I left it out. R2 does not say which three slipper lobsters, so I did not name them.

input.text: If you are a harbor seal or a California sea lion, your eyes adjust to the dark quickly and end up more sensitive to light than a human's, and if you are a northern elephant seal, you finish adjusting in less than half the time they take. If you are a harp seal, your eyes become close to a hundred million times more sensitive during dark adaptation. Nobody has measured how well you see in dim light if you are a whale, a dolphin, a manatee, or any other seal or sea lion.
input.note: The row list gives California sea lion grade i, but R4's quote states it was measured, so I named it as measured. Please check the grade. The harp seal figure is 8 log units, written as about a hundred million times.

input.text: In the red bread mold, light makes cells produce carotenoid pigment, and blue light works best. A review reports that the stalk of the mold Phycomyces also bends toward blue light. Nobody has measured which colors you sense, so whether blue matters most to you is unknown.
input.note: Left out the 450 nm figure because it has no comparison job here; R2 is from an abstract, so it is worded as a review report.

input.text: If you are a golden shiner, your eyes together cover about 335 degrees of the horizontal circle around you, and the two eyes overlap in a narrow wedge about 30 degrees wide straight ahead. Nobody has measured either width in most other fish, including bluegill, carp and trout, so nobody knows how much of the circle you see.
input.note: Only the golden shiner has records; other species are stated as unmeasured. Zebrafish figure in R2 left out.

input.text: If you are a sand-dwelling scorpion, Paruroctonus mesaensis, slit-shaped organs on your legs respond to ripples in the sand from insects as far as 50 centimeters away, according to a paper's abstract. A review reports that scorpions have hairs on the body and pedipalps that react to air streams and sense which way the air moves. Nobody has measured either sense in most species, so how far your own legs and hairs reach is unknown.
input.note: Left out R1, R2 and R5 (R2 and R1 are single-species behavior tests; R5 repeats R3). R3 is from an abstract and R4 from a review, so the row says so.

input.text: If you are a bigfin reef squid, the edges of the pupils and retinas of your two eyes add up to a field about 320 degrees wide, almost a full circle, measured in squid 63 days old. In Sepia esculenta, a cuttlefish, both eyes see the same area over about 85 degrees at the front, and you very likely have a similar overlap if you are another Sepia cuttlefish. If you are an octopus, nobody has measured how wide your field is, and a review reports that some researchers dispute that your two eyes overlap at all.
input.note: Left out R3: its 177 degrees for the European common cuttlefish is an old estimate that model calculations say is far too large, so no value is stated.

input.text: If you are a lion, tiger, leopard, jaguar, snow leopard, cheetah, mountain lion or jaguarundi, the dark opening of each eye is a round circle, where a domestic cat's is a vertical slit. If you are a clouded leopard, your pupils are vertical. If you are a Sunda clouded leopard, you very likely have vertical pupils too, since the clouded leopard, your close relative, does.
input.note: Clouded leopard (R9) has vertical pupils, unlike the other big cats, so the row names it separately.

input.text: If you are a Dampier's fiddler crab, your eyes at night respond to a flash of light about a thousand times dimmer than the flash they need in the day. Nobody has measured how well you see in the dark if you are any other crab, crayfish or shrimp in this view.
input.note: Left out R2 (deep-sea shrimp) and R3 (Leptograpsus): their figures are calculated, in other species, and numbers do not travel; R3's value has no stated unit.

input.text: After dark, about 60% of common pill-bugs are out and moving, and the other 40% are not. That comes from a field experiment on the common pill-bug, Armadillidium vulgare. Nobody has measured how active you are at night if you are another kind of woodlouse.
input.note: R2's value also gives 92% for Philoscia muscorum, but the quote states only the 60% figure and the species list marks that species as unknown, so I left it out.

input.text: You have no eyes, yet light still changes what you do. If you are a dog vomit slime mold, you cannot form your fruiting bodies without light, and in Physarum polycephalum a phytochrome, a light-sensing molecule, is one receptor for the light that makes the slime break into pieces. For most other slime molds, nobody has measured whether you sense light or which colors of it count.
input.note: R3 (Didymium iridis, light needed for sporulation) left out to keep the row short; it is grade g and could be added.

input.text: Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a garden snail or one of most other land snails and slugs. A review of their eyes says they are likely to measure only the average light over wide angles, and not to pick out fine detail. A second review reports that the slug Arion rufus needed an object about 50 degrees wide before it responded, so if you are a black slug or a Spanish slug, you very likely see about that coarsely.
input.note: Rewrite needed if the owner dislikes "and not to pick out"; R4's quote does not state a usable value, so the periwinkle figure was left out.

input.text: Many harvestmen, but not all, have a pair of eyes with a lens in the hard outer layer, set on a small tower in the middle of the back. If you are a European harvestman, a review of gene-expression work reports that you also have a hidden inner pair of side eyes and a second hidden pair of median eyes. For other harvestmen nobody has recorded how many eyes you have, and nobody has measured what kind of eyes they are or how well they see.
input.note: R1's value is cut off, so I used only the pairs its quote and value name. I did not total the eyes.

input.text: If you are a swellshark or a Scyliorhinus retifer catshark, your eye has a single visual pigment, and in the Australian swellshark no cone opsin was detected at all. A review reports a cone pigment in the dusky, blue, tiger, gummy and Port Jackson sharks, and two measured rays have three kinds of cone. Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell most sharks have, so what color looks like to you is unknown.
input.note: Left out the Greenland shark (R1) and the numbers, since none compare or picture anything here.

input.text: Only one tick has been tested for color, the tropical bont tick, Amblyomma variegatum. In a test of which colors of light steer its movement, it had a single peak of sensitivity, in blue. Nobody has measured which colors you sense, or whether you sense more than one.
input.note: Left out the 480 nm figure since it has no comparison job; R1 is a behavioral test, so it is not carried to other species.

input.text: If you are a douroucouli, a review reports that your eyes have only one kind of color-sensing cone, where a human has three. If you are Azara's night monkey or a northern lesser galago, you very likely have just one kind as well, because a table lists a single kind for owl monkeys and for the bushbabies of the genus Galago. Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of the brown greater galago.
input.note: No record covers the brown greater galago or color vision in other monkeys and apes, so the row says only what is known for night monkeys and galagos.

input.text: In the dimmest light, an owl's eye can come close to what physics allows.
