A review of behavioral studies reports that in the tawny owl, both the faintest light it can see and the detail it can make out in dim light are close to the theoretical limit. If you belong to the same genus, Strix, like the barred owl, you very likely see in the dark about as well, and for other owls nobody has measured it.
input.note: R1's value text is cut off, so I left out what sets the theoretical limit.

input.text: Picture a mole digging through the soil close to you. Nobody has measured whether you sense the shaking of that digging. In the Mediterranean medicinal leech, an abstract of nerve recordings proposes that a cell called the S cell detects water waves, and that test used water, not soil.
input.note: Left out R2: its quote reports fewer earthworms near wind turbines, which does not state that earthworms sense vibration. Also reworded the last clause if "not soil" reads as a banned contrast.

input.text: The lens inside a house cat's eye lets ultraviolet light through, about 60 percent of the ultraviolet closest to violet in the six lenses measured. Nobody has measured the lens of a lion, tiger, leopard or any other big cat, so nobody knows how much ultraviolet light gets through yours.
input.note: Lens optics travel only within a genus, so the house cat figure is not carried to big cats, despite the "rule 2" label in the species list. I left out any claim about UV-sensing cells, since no record covers them.

input.text: Nobody has measured how fast a flicker can flash before you stop seeing it as flicker. No record gives that figure for a duck, a goose or a swan, and a figure from another bird would not be yours. Humans stop seeing flicker at about 60 flashes a second, and nobody can yet say whether you see more or fewer.
input.note: No records were provided, so the row states only that the flicker limit is unmeasured; the human 60 flashes a second figure comes from the prompt.

input.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and every whale, dolphin and seal measured so far sees far less than that. If you are a harbor seal, cell counts in the retina predict about 12 under water, and the same method gives about 4 for a minke whale, a humpback whale or a walrus and about 3 for a bottlenose dolphin. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a sea lion, an elephant seal or a gray whale.
input.note: Left out killer whale, harp seal and manatee figures for brevity; the killer whale record is PARTIAL (compilation). Fin, blue and other rorquals could be carried from the minke whale but are not named.

input.text: You have no eyes, and the light that reaches you falls on a fungus and on the algae or cyanobacteria living inside it. If you are oakmoss, red light raises the activity of an enzyme, and the rise relates to a pigment in your algal partner's cells while the fungal enzyme hardly changes. If you are a scaly pelt lichen, a measurement of lichens with a cyanobacterium partner found that they make much less food in blue light than green-algal lichens do, and nobody has measured how the common orange lichen or the Christmas lichen sense light.
input.note: R1's value text is cut off; I used only what its quote states. R2 compares cyanolichens as a group, so I worded it that way.

input.text: If you are a blunt-tailed snake millipede, you can resolve a pattern of light and dark bands when one pair of bands spans about 55 degrees, which is enough to detect a dark object 20 degrees across. A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, a pattern thousands of times finer. Nobody has measured how sharply other millipedes see, though a close relative in the same genus, Cylindroiulus, very likely sees as coarsely.
input.note: Only Cylindroiulus punctatus is measured (R1, from a 56° period); the other species' sharpness is stated as unmeasured.

input.text: Some fishes have a color-sensing cell tuned to ultraviolet, light that humans cannot see at all: a review reports one in goldfish near 355 nanometers, and measurements found one near 365 in zebrafish and in a damselfish, Pomacentrus amboinensis. If you are any other fish, nobody has measured whether you have one, and for the western mosquitofish only a prediction from its gene sequence puts one near 355. Spadefish, tautog and black sea bass were tested only from 400 to 600 nanometers, a range that stops short of ultraviolet.
input.note: Goldfish figure is from a compilation (R2, partial). Left out the bluegill/bass carry (R10) and carp (R17), since neither record gives an ultraviolet value.

input.text: If you are a mangrove box jellyfish, you avoid obstacles by sight, and you turn away once an obstacle fills a certain angle of what you see. If you are a herpes jelly, you hunt at night by swimming toward areas where your prey sets off flashes of its own light.
input.note: R1 says only "avoidance"; I wrote "turn away" loosely. The record gives no figure for the angle, so none is stated.

input.text: Your outer ears are hidden beneath the feathers of your facial disc, and a review reports that some owls can find prey by hearing alone. If you are a great gray owl, you can plunge through snow to catch prey without any visual cues. For most owls, nobody has measured how exactly you tell where a sound comes from.
input.note: No record gives a localization accuracy, so the barn owl angle figure from the example row was left out; R1 gives only sensitivity.

input.text: Your crown of feathery radioles has eyes on it. If you are an Indo-Pacific Christmas tree worm, the visual pigment in those eyes absorbs light best in the blue, at about 465 nanometers. If you are a Caribbean or California Christmas tree worm or a blue tube worm, you very likely have the same pigment, since all of you are close relatives in the same genus.
input.note: Only the Indo-Pacific species is measured; the 465 nm figure is stated for it and the others are carried within the genus.

input.text: If you are a big brown bat, you send out 5 to 10 search calls a second, each up to 15 to 20 milliseconds long. If you are a Mexican free-tailed bat, you send out about 4 a second, each about 14 milliseconds long. Nobody has measured the search calls of most other bats, so for them these figures are unknown.
input.note: Left out R1, R3, R4 (other measured species, but about resolution, range and beam width, not call timing) and R8 (a g record for a different species).

input.text: Picture the stretch of the world you take in at one time, from the left edge to the right edge. Nobody has measured how wide that stretch is for you.
input.note: Left out R1 (Amblyomma variegatum, 43 degrees): its quote gives two values for Amblyomma without saying which belongs to which species, and field width travels only within a genus.

input.text: When a shadow falls over you, a nerve of yours fires a long burst. If you are an Atlantic surf clam, each of your pallial nerves has one light-sensitive fiber that goes silent in the light. When the light stops, that fiber sends a prolonged burst of impulses at high frequency.
input.note: R1 gives no firing rate, so I left out any number.

input.text: A human reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart, and your eyes see much coarser detail than that. If you are a black, grey-headed or little red flying fox, counts of nerve cells in your eye put your sharpness at between 4 and 6 cycles a degree, a fifth of a human's or less. If you are a Madagascan rousette, the estimate is about 3, roughly a tenth of a human's.
input.note: Grey-headed has two figures (about 4 in R1, 5.5 in R3), so I gave a 4 to 6 range. I left out the Egyptian rousette, because R1 lists it but its quote does not state a value for it.

input.text: If you are a red fox or an arctic fox, you have two kinds of color-sensing cell, where a human has three. Most of yours sense middle to long wavelengths of light and a minority sense short wavelengths, which makes your color vision dichromatic. Nobody has counted these cells in a gray fox or an island fox.
input.note: Left out the 555 nm peak (R1-R3): its quote says "one cone pigment", which does not match two cone classes, and the number had no job.

input.text: A flatfish buried in sand gives off a faint electric field, and if you are a small-spotted catshark, you find it by that field alone and give the same feeding response to two buried electrodes. If you are a scalloped hammerhead, a juvenile turns toward a prey-like electric field from about 30 centimeters away. Electric sense has been measured in only a few sharks, rays and rabbit fish, and for most others, including you if you are none of these, nobody has measured it.
input.note: Left out pore counts (R4-R6) and cell firing (R1) to stay within three sentences; "centimeters" used for the 30 cm figure.

input.text: If you are a red fox or an arctic fox, your pupil is a narrow vertical slit. If you are a gray fox, your pupil is oval, unlike the slits of foxes in the genus Vulpes, such as the red fox.
input.note: Left out R4-R13: their quotes are classification codes that do not state the pupil shape. R13 (island fox, "Vertical") also conflicts with R1 for the genus Urocyon, so I did not describe island, Tibetan sand or Rüppell's foxes.

input.text: If you are a lone star tick, you sense carbon dioxide, and the signal lasts longer when you have been kept in air low in carbon dioxide than in air high in it. If you are a blacklegged tick, the pores in your Haller's organ respond most to m-cresol and next most to p-cresol. Nobody has measured what the other ticks sense this way, so for you the rest is unknown.
input.note: Left out R3 (castor bean tick questing time and dryness): it is about humidity, not chemical sensing. Left out the female detail in R1 because the quote does not state it.

input.text: If you are a lone star tick, your sensing cells respond electrically to carbon dioxide, a gas animals breathe out. If you are a blacklegged tick, the sensors in your Haller's organ respond most strongly to a chemical called m-cresol, and next most to p-cresol. Nobody has measured which chemicals you sense if you are any other kind of tick.
input.note: Left out R3 (castor bean tick questing time and dryness) because it does not state a chemical sense; did not say where cresols come from since no record states it.

input.text: If you are a harbor seal, your eyes held still take in about 210 degrees from side to side, and both eyes see the same part of it over about 65 degrees. If you are a spotted seal, you very likely see about the same, since the harbor seal is a close relative in the same genus. Nobody has measured how wide you see if you are any other whale, dolphin or seal.
input.note: Only the harbor seal has records for this row. The spotted seal line carries within the genus Phoca. No record supports a human comparison figure for field width, so none is given.

input.text: If you are a red fox, you hear tones from about 50 hertz up to about 48,000 hertz, a span of almost 10 octaves. That comes from hearing tests with three red foxes, and nobody has measured the hearing of the other kinds of fox.
input.note: No record gives a human hearing range, so the row makes no comparison with a human.

input.text: If you are a pale spear-nosed bat, your echolocation cannot separate two directions that are closer together than about 8 degrees, which is roughly four human thumbs held side by side at arm's length. In bats that call through the mouth, the beam of sound narrows when the bat enters a confined space and widens within dozens of milliseconds when it flies toward open space. Nobody has measured how finely you can tell where an echo comes from unless you are that one species.
input.note: R1's quote shows "80" where the degree sign was lost; I used the record's value of 8 degrees. Beam-width records for Daubenton's bat (R4) describe the call, not direction resolution, so I left them out.

input.text: A lamp flashing 60 times a second looks steady to a human, and the sharks measured so far stop seeing flicker at lower rates than that. If you are a brownbanded bamboo shark, the limit is about 45 flashes a second, if you are a blacknose shark it is about 15, and if you are a small-spotted catshark it is about 3. Nobody has measured it in most sharks and rays, so for them the number is unknown.
input.note: Left out the ranges in rays (R17 reaches 60 Hz) to keep the sentence true; said "sharks measured" only.

input.text: Scorpions have two kinds of eyes, and a review reports that the median eyes may form low-resolution images, while the lateral eyes are highly sensitive to light but have no lens that forms an image. Nobody has measured the eyes of your species, so what each kind does for you is not known.
input.note: Left out R1 (a whipscorpion, a different order) and the numbers in R2 and R3, since they belong to single species.

input.text: Every bat measured so far sees far less fine detail than a human, who reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart. If you are a brown big-eared bat, a table of measurements reports about 1 cycle a degree, and if you are a great fruit-eating bat, a count of the cells in your retina gives about 2. For most other bats, nobody has measured how sharply you see.
input.note: Left out other species' figures (vampire bat, Daubenton's bat, etc.) to keep the row short; big brown bat's R16 left out because its row grade is i.

input.text: The Asian shore crab has two kinds of color-sensing pigment, one tuned to violet-blue light and one to green, and you very likely have two as well. A review reports two kinds in the red swamp crawfish too, with the second reaching into yellow and orange light, while in the main cells of four fiddler crabs only one kind has been found.
input.note: Fiddler crab record (R8) shows one class in main cells, so I named it as an exception; numbers left out since they have no comparison job.

input.text: If you are the sea slug Berghia stephanieae, you crawl toward a black stripe set outside the arena where you are placed. A meeting abstract reports that Berghia reliably reached the stripe.
input.note: R1's value is cut off at a second stripe test ("isolumin..."), and the quote does not state it, so I left that part out. I also left out other sea slugs, since no record covers them.

input.text: Nobody has measured how many kinds of color-sensing cell you have, or which colors they pick up. Nobody can yet say whether you see color at all.
input.note: No records were supplied, so the row only states that nothing has been measured; I left out any claim about millipede eyes or light sensing.

input.text: The abstract of a study reports that one millipede, Paraspirobolus lucifugus, avoids light and is active only at night, and that its activity rhythm is apparently governed by an internal clock. Nobody has recorded whether you are active at night or by day.
input.note: Only one record, from an abstract about one species; nothing on the listed species, so the row stays grade i.

input.text: If you are a horned ghost crab, a band across each eye level with the horizon is about 30 degrees high, and at its finest your eye samples four times more finely up and down than side to side. The fiddler crab Uca lactea has a band like this too, running around the middle of its eyes. Nobody has measured whether you have one unless you are one of those crabs or a close relative of the ghost crab.
input.note: Left out the mantis shrimp records (not crabs) and R4, whose quoted value does not state a horizon band.

input.text: If you are a lungless salamander, such as a red-backed, slimy or two-lined salamander, a groove runs from each of your nostrils down to your upper lip. Nobody has measured how well you smell, and that goes for newts and the other salamanders too.
input.note: R1's value text is cut off at "nose tapping draws", and its quote only states the grooves, so I left out any claim about nose tapping or the vomeronasal organ.
